title: Presentation Skills
description: Structure and deliver talks with Minto/SCQA, evidence-based slide design, honest data stories, and strong Q&A.

questions.prompt: You have 10 minutes with the CFO to recommend consolidating two warehouses into one. Following Barbara Minto's Pyramid Principle, how should you open?

options.text: With the history of the warehouse network so she has full context
With the recommendation and its main reason, e.g. a $2.1M annual saving
With the analysis method so she trusts the numbers before seeing them
With an agenda slide listing the six sections you plan to cover

questions.explanation: The pyramid puts the governing thought (the answer) at the top, followed by the supporting arguments, so a busy executive gets the point even if time runs out. Building up through history or method makes her wait for the one thing she needs to decide on.

questions.prompt: Each of a trainer's slides shows a process diagram plus a full paragraph of text, which she reads aloud word for word. Based on Richard Mayer's multimedia learning research, what change will help the audience learn most?

options.text: Add more detail to the paragraph so people can read ahead at their own pace
Remove the diagram so that attention stays on the text she is reading aloud
Keep the diagram, cut the paragraph to a short label, and give the detail by voice
Hand out printed copies of the slides beforehand so people can read along

questions.explanation: Mayer's redundancy principle shows people learn better from graphics plus narration than from graphics, narration, and the same printed text, which competes for visual attention. Removing the diagram throws away the multimedia benefit of pairing words with pictures.

questions.prompt: You need to show the leadership team monthly active users over the last 24 months and point out a sharp dip in month 14. Which chart fits this message?

options.text: A line chart with the 24 months in order along the x-axis
A pie chart with one slice for each of the 24 months
A horizontal bar chart sorted from highest to lowest month
A table that lists the exact value for each of the 24 months

questions.explanation: Line charts show change over continuous time, so the trend and the dip are visible at a glance. Sorting bars by value destroys the time order that the dip depends on, and a table makes the audience find the pattern themselves.

questions.prompt: Using the assertion-evidence slide design studied by Michael Alley and colleagues, which headline should replace "Q3 Churn" on a slide whose chart shows churn by customer segment?

options.text: Q3 Churn by Customer Segment
Churn Analysis: Q3 Results and Overview
Q3 churn data (source: CRM export, Oct 2)
SMB churn doubled in Q3; enterprise held steady

questions.explanation: Assertion-evidence slides use a full-sentence headline stating the takeaway, with the visual as evidence; research found audiences understand and remember more than with topic-phrase titles. Options a to c are still topic labels that leave the audience to work out the point.

questions.prompt: True or false: When an audience member asks a question you cannot answer, you protect your credibility best by giving your best guess confidently rather than admitting you do not know.
questions.explanation: A confident guess that turns out wrong damages credibility far more than an honest "I don't know, and I'll find out by Friday." Committing to a specific follow-up keeps trust and gets the person a correct answer.

questions.prompt: Arrange these opening sentences for a pitch to the support director in Minto's SCQA order (Situation, Complication, Question, Answer).

lines.text: Our support team handles 12,000 tickets a month with a 4-hour average response time.
Since the spring launch, ticket volume is up 40% and response times have doubled.
So how do we get back to 4-hour responses without doubling headcount?
Launch self-service for the top five ticket types, which make up 45% of volume.

questions.explanation: SCQA starts with an uncontroversial situation, introduces the complication that disrupts it, raises the question the complication creates, and then gives the answer, which becomes the top of the pyramid. Putting the 40% increase first removes the baseline that makes it meaningful.

questions.prompt: A slide shows an engine diagram with nine parts numbered 1 to 9; the key explaining the numbers is on the next slide. According to Mayer's spatial contiguity principle, what is the fix?

options.text: Put each part's name next to that part on the diagram itself
Enlarge the numbers on the diagram so they are easier to see
Move the key to the handout so the slides stay uncluttered
Color-code the parts and put a color key on the following slide

questions.explanation: Spatial contiguity says people learn better when words are placed near the parts of the graphic they describe, so they do not spend working memory matching numbers to a distant key. Color codes on another slide keep the same split-attention problem.

questions.prompt: You have a 20-minute slot at a board meeting to request funding for a data platform. Select all practices that fit an executive audience.

options.text: State the recommendation and the funding ask within the first minute
Put detailed methodology and data in backup slides or an appendix
Walk through the analysis in the order you did it to build credibility
Prepare a version that makes the core case in five minutes if cut short
Save the ask for the final slide so the board hears the full case first

questions.explanation: Executives want the answer and the decision up front, detail available on demand, and a presenter who can adapt when agendas run long. Chronological walkthroughs and a last-slide ask risk running out of time before the board learns what you need.

questions.prompt: Following Cole Nussbaumer Knaflic's storytelling-with-data guidance, how should this chart be redesigned?

code.source:
Chart:   Quarterly revenue by product line, Q1-Q4
Type:    line chart, 6 lines, each in a different bright color
Legend:  right side, alphabetical
Title:   "Revenue by Product Line"
Message: Product C is the only line that declined.

options.text: Add data labels to all 24 points so the audience can compare every value
Apply a 3D effect so the six lines are easier to tell apart from one another
Gray out five lines, color and label C directly, and title the chart with the takeaway
Split it into six small charts, one per product, keeping the same bright colors

questions.explanation: Knaflic recommends decluttering and using a preattentive attribute such as color sparingly to direct attention to the one series that carries the message, with a title that states it. Labeling all 24 points adds clutter and still leaves the audience to find Product C.

questions.prompt: A draft slide shows customer satisfaction as a bar chart: Region A 97.1, Region B 97.9, Region C 98.4. The y-axis runs from 96.5 to 98.5, so Region C's bar looks about three times as tall as Region A's. What is the problem and fix?

options.text: Three regions are too few for bars; show them as a pie chart instead
Bar length encodes value, so start the axis at zero or switch to a dot plot
Gridlines are missing; add them so readers can see the exact values
Nothing needs fixing, since the axis range is labeled on the chart

questions.explanation: Viewers judge bars by length, so a truncated baseline turns a 1.3-point gap into an apparent threefold difference. If the small differences matter, a dot plot can use a narrow range honestly because it encodes value by position, not length.

questions.prompt: During Q&A at a 30-person all-hands, one manager asks a detailed question about how the new tool handles her team's specific billing codes. A full answer would take ten minutes and matters to no one else. What should you do?

options.text: Answer it fully now, since every question deserves the same amount of time
Tell her the question is off-topic for this forum and take the next one
Ask the audience whether anyone else knows the answer to her question
Give a brief answer, offer a detailed follow-up afterward, and move on

questions.explanation: Respecting both the questioner and the group means acknowledging the question, giving what is useful in a sentence or two, and committing to a specific follow-up. A ten-minute answer spends everyone's time on one person's need, and dismissing her as off-topic damages trust.

questions.prompt: Two slides into your 12-slide proposal, the CFO interrupts: "What will this cost?" The cost breakdown is on slide 9. What should you do?

options.text: Give the headline cost in a sentence now, then resume from slide 3
Say "Great question, I'll cover that on slide 9" and keep going
Skip ahead to slide 9 and present the remaining slides from there
Ask her to hold questions until the end so the story stays intact

questions.explanation: Executives signal what matters to their decision through their questions; answering immediately and briefly (answer first) keeps their attention and trust, and you can still present the breakdown on slide 9. Deferring leaves the decision-maker distracted for seven slides, and jumping to slide 9 abandons the structure the rest of the case depends on.

questions.prompt: Your forecasting model produced the output below. The COO says, "Just give me one number." Which statement should go on your summary slide?

code.source:
Projected annual savings, route optimization
  P10:  $3.1M
  P50:  $3.8M
  P90:  $4.6M
Largest driver of the range: diesel price

options.text: We will save $3,847,212 per year with route optimization.
About $3.8M a year, likely $3.1M to $4.6M, driven mainly by diesel prices.
Savings can't be reliably predicted, so we'll share a number after the pilot.
Route optimization will save up to $4.6M a year at current diesel prices.

questions.explanation: Lead with the central estimate the COO asked for, but keep the range and its main driver so the decision accounts for uncertainty. An unrounded figure implies false precision, and "up to $4.6M" quotes the optimistic P90 as if it were the expectation.

questions.prompt: A colleague's slide is described below. What should be changed before it goes to the executive team?

code.source:
Title:      "Marketing spend drives signups"
Chart:      dual-axis line chart, Jan-Dec
Left axis:  Marketing spend ($K), 0 to 500    (spend rose from 120 to 360)
Right axis: Signups, 9,000 to 10,000          (signups rose from 9,100 to 9,600)
Visual:     the two lines rise together and overlap almost exactly

options.text: Swap the left and right axes so that marketing spend is on the right side
Add a legend so viewers can tell which line belongs to which axis
Use a thicker, darker line for signups so it stands out from spend
Index both to a common baseline or use two panels, and drop the causal title

questions.explanation: With two independently chosen axis ranges, a 200% rise in spend and a roughly 5% rise in signups look identical, and the title claims causation the chart cannot show. Indexing to a baseline or using separate panels shows the true relative change; a legend fixes labeling but not the distortion.

questions.prompt: Your recommendation, to be decided at Thursday's executive meeting, cuts the Operations VP's budget by 15%. She has not seen the analysis. What should you do before Thursday?

options.text: Nothing; present it Thursday so every executive hears it at the same time
Remove the budget impact from the deck to avoid conflict in the meeting
Pre-wire it: walk her through the analysis privately and hear her objections
Email the full deck to all executives the night before, with no discussion

questions.explanation: Pre-wiring key stakeholders, especially those most affected, lets you surface objections, correct errors, and adjust the proposal before the decision meeting instead of having the VP blindsided in front of peers. Hiding the budget impact undermines trust and the decision itself.
